title: Changes of state and latent heat — energy that doesn't raise temperature
examTip: E = mL is the key equation. There are two types. Latent heat of FUSION is for melting or freezing. Latent heat of VAPORISATION is for boiling or condensing. Vaporisation needs far more energy, because the particles must be fully separated.
introTips: Steam at 100°C causes much worse burns than boiling water at 100°C. Latent heat explains exactly why.
Sweating cools you down well because water has an enormous latent heat of vaporisation.
The flat sections on a heating curve are a favourite exam graph question. You need to explain what is happening at each one.
intro: Once the water in a kettle reaches 100°C, it still takes ages to boil away. The temperature isn't rising. But the energy isn't disappearing. It is pulling water molecules away from each other as the liquid turns to steam. This 'hidden' energy changes the state without changing the temperature. It is called latent heat. It explains why steam burns are so bad. It explains how your fridge keeps food cold. It also explains why sweating on a hot day works.

keyPoints.heading: Temperature during changes of state — the heating curve
keyPoints.content: When you heat a substance, its temperature usually rises. But something interesting happens at its melting point or boiling point. The temperature stays constant, even though energy is still going in. You can see this on a heating curve. This is a graph of temperature against time (or energy added): - Sloping sections: the temperature is rising, and the kinetic energy of the particles is increasing - Flat sections: the temperature is constant, because a change of state is happening At a flat section: - The particles are taking in energy - This energy overcomes the forces of attraction between the particles - The particles gain potential energy (not kinetic energy) - No increase in kinetic energy → no increase in temperature This energy is called latent heat. 'Latent' means 'hidden'. The energy is there, but you can't see it on the thermometer. When the substance cools, the reverse happens. Latent heat is released during freezing and condensation. The flat sections appear again, at the same temperatures.
writeBullets: During a change of state, temperature stays CONSTANT, even though energy is going in
Energy during a change of state → overcomes forces between particles → increases potential energy
No increase in kinetic energy → no rise in temperature
Heating curve: sloping = temperature rising. Flat = change of state
Latent heat — 'hidden' energy taken in or released during a change of state
Flat sections appear at the melting point AND the boiling point

keyTerms.def: Energy absorbed or released during a change of state — does not cause a temperature change
A graph of temperature vs time (or energy) showing flat sections at melting and boiling points

keyPoints.memTip: Latent = hidden. The energy is there, but you can't see it on a thermometer. It is overcoming the forces between particles, not heating them up.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Draw a full heating curve for ice → water → steam. Label all 5 sections: solid heating, melting, liquid heating, boiling, gas heating.

keyPoints.heading: Specific latent heat — the equation E = mL
keyPoints.content: Specific latent heat (L) is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance. The temperature does not change. Equation: E = mL Where: E = energy (J), m = mass (kg), L = specific latent heat (J/kg) Rearrangements: L = E/m   m = E/L Two types: Specific latent heat of fusion (L_f): the energy per kg to melt or freeze a substance. This is solid ↔ liquid - Water: L_f = 334,000 J/kg (334 kJ/kg) Specific latent heat of vaporisation (L_v): the energy per kg to boil or condense a substance. This is liquid ↔ gas - Water: L_v = 2,260,000 J/kg (2260 kJ/kg) Why is L_v so much bigger than L_f? Melting only partly overcomes the forces between particles. The particles still stay close. Vaporisation fully overcomes the forces between particles. The particles must be completely separated and moved far apart. This needs a much bigger increase in potential energy. So much more energy is needed.
writeBullets: Specific latent heat (L) — the energy per kg to change state. Unit: J/kg
E = mL (energy = mass × specific latent heat)
Latent heat of fusion — melting or freezing (solid ↔ liquid). Water: 334,000 J/kg
Latent heat of vaporisation — boiling or condensing (liquid ↔ gas). Water: 2,260,000 J/kg
Vaporisation needs far more energy than fusion. The particles must be completely separated
Rearrangements: L = E/m and m = E/L

keyTerms.def: Energy per kg needed to melt (or freeze) a substance at constant temperature. Unit: J/kg
Energy per kg needed to boil (or condense) a substance at constant temperature. Unit: J/kg
Energy = mass × specific latent heat. The equation for calculating energy in a change of state

keyPoints.memTip: Fusion = melting (think of fusing solid particles into a liquid). Vaporisation = boiling (vapour = gas).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Don't mix up fusion (melting) with nuclear fusion. Also, the value of L for water is given in exams. You don't need to learn the numbers.

keyPoints.heading: Calculations using E = mL
keyPoints.content: The equation E = mL is simple. But take care with units and rearrangements. Worked example 1 — melting ice How much energy is needed to melt 2 kg of ice at 0°C? L_f (water) = 334,000 J/kg E = mL = 2 × 334,000 = 668,000 J = 668 kJ Worked example 2 — condensing steam How much energy is released when 0.5 kg of steam condenses to water at 100°C? L_v (water) = 2,260,000 J/kg E = mL = 0.5 × 2,260,000 = 1,130,000 J = 1130 kJ (Released, because condensation is exothermic) Worked example 3 — finding specific latent heat 500 g of a substance takes in 150,000 J while melting at constant temperature. L = E/m = 150,000 / 0.5 = 300,000 J/kg Combined calculation — heating ice to steam To turn 1 kg of ice at -10°C into steam at 100°C: 1. Heat ice from -10°C to 0°C: Q = mcΔT = 1 × 2100 × 10 = 21,000 J 2. Melt ice at 0°C: Q = mL_f = 1 × 334,000 = 334,000 J 3. Heat water from 0°C to 100°C: Q = mcΔT = 1 × 4200 × 100 = 420,000 J 4. Boil water at 100°C: Q = mL_v = 1 × 2,260,000 = 2,260,000 J Total = 3,035,000 J ≈ 3 MJ
writeBullets: E = mL. Put mass in kg and L in J/kg to get energy in J
To condense 0.5 kg steam: E = 0.5 × 2,260,000 = 1,130,000 J (released)
Rearrange for L: L = E/m. Remember to convert mass to kg
Combined problems: add up Q = mcΔT for temperature changes AND E = mL for changes of state
Say whether energy is taken in (melting or boiling) or released (freezing or condensing)

keyTerms.def: Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg°C — used alongside latent heat in combined heating calculations
Energy is released to surroundings — freezing and condensation release latent heat
Energy is absorbed from surroundings — melting and boiling absorb latent heat

keyPoints.memTip: E = mL for changes of state. Q = mcΔT for temperature changes.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Remember to convert 500 g to 0.5 kg before substituting. Unit errors are the main trap in E = mL calculations.

keyPoints.heading: Applications of latent heat
keyPoints.content: Latent heat is not just theory. It has important uses, and some of them save lives. Sweating and cooling: sweat is mainly water. Its specific latent heat of vaporisation is very high: 2260 kJ/kg. Sweat evaporates from your skin. It carries an enormous amount of energy away from your body. This is why sweating cools you so well, even in very hot weather. Steam burns: steam at 100°C causes far worse burns than boiling water at 100°C. Both are at the same temperature, so why? When steam condenses on skin, it releases its latent heat of vaporisation onto the skin. That is 2260 kJ/kg. This comes on top of the heat from cooling down from 100°C. This extra 2260 kJ/kg makes steam burns much more serious. Refrigerators: a working fluid (refrigerant) is pumped around a circuit. Inside the fridge it evaporates. It takes in latent heat from the contents, which cools them. Outside the fridge it condenses. It releases that latent heat to the surroundings. This is why the back of a fridge is warm. The refrigerator is really pumping heat from inside to outside. Freeze-drying food: food is frozen. Then it is put somewhere with low pressure, so the ice sublimates straight to vapour. This preserves the food without heat damage.
writeBullets: Sweating — water has a high L_v. So evaporation carries huge amounts of energy away from the body
Steam burns — condensing steam releases 2260 kJ/kg of latent heat onto skin. This is on top of the heat from cooling
Steam at 100°C causes worse burns than water at 100°C for the same reason
Refrigerator — refrigerant evaporates inside, taking in latent heat and cooling the contents. It condenses outside, releasing heat
The back of a fridge is warm because latent heat is released there during condensation
Freeze-drying — ice sublimes to vapour at low pressure. This preserves food without high temperatures

keyTerms.def: The working fluid in a refrigerator that evaporates and condenses as it cycles, transferring heat from inside to outside
Removing water from food by sublimation under low pressure — preserves food without cooking it

keyPoints.memTip: Steam burns = DOUBLE the energy. You get L_v as it condenses, THEN Q = mcΔT as it cools. It is always worse than the same mass of boiling water.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The refrigerator explanation is a classic 6-mark question. Practise writing it in full. It evaporates inside, taking in latent heat. It condenses outside, releasing it.

tables.title: Summary of latent heat types
rows: Forces between particles weaken; particles free to move past each other
Forces pull particles back together; particles lock into lattice
Forces between particles overcome; particles far apart
Forces pull particles back together; particles close together again

0.question: A heating curve has a flat section at the melting point. What is happening there?
options: The substance is melting. The energy raises the particles' potential energy, not their kinetic energy
The heater has stopped, so no energy is going in
The particles are speeding up, so the temperature is rising
The particles are being destroyed as the solid melts
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Energy is still going in, but the temperature stays the same. The energy overcomes the forces between particles.
0.wrongFeedback: Energy is still going in at a flat section. It overcomes the forces between particles. Potential energy rises, kinetic energy does not. So the temperature stays the same.

1.question: What does the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water tell you?
options: The energy needed to turn 1 kg of liquid water into steam, with no change in temperature
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C
The energy needed to melt 1 kg of ice
The temperature at which water boils
1.correctFeedback: Correct. Vaporisation is liquid to gas. Specific latent heat is the energy per kilogram, with no temperature change.
1.wrongFeedback: Vaporisation means liquid to gas. Specific latent heat is the energy to change the state of 1 kg. The temperature does not change. Raising the temperature by 1 °C is specific heat capacity.

2.question: How much energy is needed to melt 3 kg of ice at 0°C? (L_f of water = 334,000 J/kg)
2.correctFeedback: Correct! E = mL = 3 × 334,000 = 1,002,000 J = 1002 kJ. The temperature stays at 0°C the whole time. All this energy overcomes the forces between particles. None of it raises the temperature.
2.wrongFeedback: Use E = mL. Multiply the mass (3 kg) by the specific latent heat of fusion (334,000 J/kg). That gives 3 × 334,000 = 1,002,000 J.

3.question: Steam at 100°C causes worse burns than boiling water at 100°C. They are at the same temperature. Why are steam burns worse?
options: When steam condenses on skin, it releases its latent heat of vaporisation (2260 kJ/kg). This adds to the energy from cooling
Steam moves faster, so it has more kinetic energy than water at the same temperature
Steam is hotter than the water, even though the thermometer shows 100°C
Steam has more particles per unit volume than liquid water
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right. Steam condensing on skin releases an extra 2260 kJ/kg of latent heat. This happens before it even starts to cool. This extra energy is what makes steam so much more dangerous.
3.wrongFeedback: Steam and boiling water are both at 100°C. Their particles have the same kinetic energy. The key difference is latent heat. When steam condenses, it releases 2260 kJ/kg onto the skin before cooling. Water has no latent heat to release. It just cools.

commonMistakes: Thinking temperature rises during a change of state. It stays constant while the energy overcomes the forces between particles. Potential energy increases, but kinetic energy does not.
Mixing up latent heat of fusion with nuclear fusion. Here, 'fusion' means melting or freezing (solid ↔ liquid).
Using mass in grams instead of kg in E = mL. Always convert to kg first by dividing grams by 1000.
Forgetting that condensation and freezing RELEASE latent heat. Energy goes from the substance to the surroundings.
In combined calculations, forgetting to include both kinds of step. You need the latent heat steps (E = mL) AND the temperature-change steps (Q = mcΔT).
examTips: When asked about a flat section on a heating curve, say the temperature is constant. The energy is overcoming the forces of attraction between particles. This increases potential energy, not kinetic energy.
In E = mL calculations, always convert mass to kg. Check you use the right L. Use fusion for melting or freezing. Use vaporisation for boiling or condensing.
For questions on uses, like sweating, steam burns and fridges, explain three things. Say which change of state is happening. Say whether energy is taken in or released. Say what effect this has.
revisionCardBullets: Latent heat — energy taken in or released during a change of state. The temperature does not change
Temperature stays CONSTANT during a change of state
Energy during a change of state → overcomes forces between particles → increases potential energy (not kinetic)
E = mL (energy = mass × specific latent heat). Unit of L: J/kg
Latent heat of fusion — melting or freezing (solid ↔ liquid). Water: 334,000 J/kg
Latent heat of vaporisation — boiling or condensing (liquid ↔ gas). Water: 2,260,000 J/kg
L_v >> L_f, because vaporisation fully separates all the particles (much more potential energy)
Sweating cools the body. High L_v means evaporation removes a large amount of energy
Steam burns worse than boiling water. Condensing releases 2260 kJ/kg of latent heat onto skin
Refrigerator — refrigerant evaporates inside (takes in heat) and condenses outside (releases heat)
